newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Cartel ruling clears Allianz takeovers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Cartel ruling clears Allianz takeovers.

text.p: Allianz AG Holding on Tuesday got the green light for a full takeover of the Vereinte Holding AG insurance group, after a canny deal aimed at appeasing cartel office worries but still giving it a strong role in the lucrative German health insurance market.

Europe's largest insurer earlier this year deflected concerns that the Vereinte takeover would give it a stranglehold on the German health insurance market by selling its existing health unit, Deutsche Krankenversicherungs AG.

In response to this surprising move, the German cartel office on Tuesday said it had approved Allianz's plans to take 100 percent control of Vereinte and its related plan to buy the biggest German loan insurer, Hermes Kreditversicherungs AG.
Allianz welcomed the move, which had been widely expected, and said its way was now clear to fully integrate the units.

"This means we now own Vereinte and Hermes in full, we are in charge and we can quickly implement all the plans we have developed to integrate them into the Allianz group," Allianz spokesman Emilio Galli-Zugaro told Reuters.

Allianz's 10,000-strong sales team would start selling Vereinte products from January 1, 1997 and plans could now proceed to finance Hermes' expansion abroad -- a move it needs to survive in the deregulated European market.
"The Hermes takeover is a tremendous help to us in keeping a leading edge in industrial insurance," Galli-Zugaro said.
The EU Commission, which has already sanctioned the Hermes takeover, has also approved Allianz's plans for Vereinte, sources there said on Tuesday.
Allianz arranged its takeover of Vereinte via a complex share swap earlier this year with close ally Muenchener Rueckversicherungs AG, or Munich Re.

The reinsurer took over DKV, the biggest European health insurer, and in return, relinquished control of Hermes, the 25 percent share of Vereinte which Allianz did not already own, and a stake in Allianz's Austrian operations.

The move was viewed as positive and pragmatic for Allianz but initially caused confusion in industry circles as Allianz had been universally expected to sell Vereinte and was understood to have held talks with several potential buyers.

Allianz got a majority stake in Vereinte in 1994 as part of a package of companies bought from Swiss Re, which also comprised Lloyd Adriatico of Italy and Elvia of Switzerland, but had never been able to exercise control on the unit.

German cartel authorities argued that ownership of both DKV and Vereinte unit Vereinte Krankenversicherungs AG, which is Germany's second largest health insurer, would have left Allianz dominating the German health insurance market.
By selling DKV but keeping Vereinte and acquiring Hermes, Allianz said it was fulfilling its own long term strategic objectives as well as easing cartel office worries.

"For example, this is adding 1.8 percent to our share of the German life insurance market and two percent to our share of the property and casualty market," spokesman Galli-Zugaro said on Tuesday, referring to Vereinte's other German units.
"One could hardly have expected this story to have such a happy ending," said Commerzbank AG analyst Patrizia Novak.

Novak also predicted that Allianz would not consolidate Vereinte, which had 7.5 billion marks premium income in 1995, into its group accounts until next year. Allianz itself said these details had not been finalised.
The German private health insurance industry is regarded as having strong long term prospects. It currently insures seven million Germans and turned in premium income of 32.1 billion marks in 1995.
